title: Kitchen Math & Meal Planning Challenge
tagline: Servings · Packages · A meal you actually eat
goal: Your kid plans one to three real meals for the family, checks what's already at home, turns the meals into a shopping list, prices it by the package, shops it and helps make it. Then the receipt goes next to the plan. It's the maths of every grocery run: what one serving costs, and what the store makes you buy.
need: A day this week when your kid plans one to three family meals
Paper and a pencil, or a notes app, and a calculator
A store flyer, receipt or grocery website for prices (the Price Menu at the end of the guide works too)
A grocery trip, and a basket for your kid to carry

lesson.text: Food has two prices: what one serving costs, and what you pay at the store. You can't buy one slice of bread. A good plan uses both.

model.line: Bread $4 + turkey $6 + cheese $5 = $15, for 1 sandwich or for 4.
Lunch for 1 really costs $15. Lunch for 4 still costs $15, with bread left over.
Use the rest of the loaf for tomorrow's toast, so nothing gets wasted.

lesson.modelNote: Serving prices make lunch for 4 look like 4 times the cost. At the store it's the same $15 either way, and the leftover loaf becomes tomorrow's toast.

howTo.intro: Use what your family eats on a normal Tuesday, not a perfect menu, and leave nutrition out of it today. You handle the stove, the oven and the knives. The plan, the list and the basket are theirs. The first plan will price servings while the store sells packages, so let them find that gap on their own.

plan.what: Check what's home, write the list and price it (Steps 1 to 3).
Cook it, eat it, then check the receipt (Step 5).

troubleshoot.q: The shopping list is a mess
troubleshoot.a: Ask 'what's actually in that sandwich?' Breaking meals into ingredients is the hardest part, and the most useful.

troubleshoot.q: The store is out of something
troubleshoot.a: Ask what would do the same job, and what it costs. Swapping on the spot is part of the skill.

steps.title: Pick the day and check what's home
steps.why: Plan from the fridge first. What's already there is already paid for.
steps.kid: Your kid picks a day this week and the meals that are theirs to plan: breakfast, lunch, dinner or a snack, one to three of them. Before choosing any food, they check the fridge and the cupboards and write down what's there and how much is left: half a loaf, 5 eggs, a bag of rice.
steps.you: Agree on the day and which meals are theirs, and keep it to food your family really eats. Say yes to simple: pasta night counts.
ask: Which meals are you planning, and for how many people?
What's already at home that you could use?
steps.tip: Check the dates while you're in there. Something that needs eating soon is the best place to start a plan.

levels.explore: Plan one meal, like lunch, and find 3 things for it already at home.
levels.develop: Plan 2 or 3 meals and list what's at home, with how much is left.
levels.extend: Plan the day around 2 things in the fridge that need eating soon, and say what each one saves.

steps.title: Turn the meals into a shopping list
steps.why: 'Sandwich' isn't on any shelf. Bread, turkey and cheese are.
steps.kid: Your kid breaks each meal into ingredients and scales them for everyone eating: 4 sandwiches is 8 slices of bread, 8 slices of turkey, 4 slices of cheese. Then they cross off what's already at home, write anything used twice only once, and sort what's left by aisle.
steps.you: Help them catch overlaps: if bread shows up at breakfast and lunch, it goes on the list once. Let them do the multiplying.
ask: What can you cross off because it's already at home?
steps.tip: Set out a plate for each person and point at what goes on it. Kids who can't picture 'servings' can count plates.

levels.explore: Set out a plate for each person at one meal, and list what goes on all of them.
levels.develop: Scale every meal for the family, cross off what's at home and sort the list by aisle.
levels.extend: Find one ingredient that can do two meals, like rice tonight and fried rice tomorrow, and show what it saves.

steps.title: Price it by the package
steps.why: The store sells packages, not servings. That's where the plan meets the till.
steps.kid: Your kid prices the shopping list using a flyer, a grocery website or the Price Menu at the end of the guide. Every line gets the package price, not the serving price: the whole loaf, the whole pack of turkey. They add it up, then work out what one plate of one meal really costs.
steps.you: Ask them to compare the list total with what they guessed one meal would cost. Let them find the gap before you explain it.
ask: What does the whole list cost?
What does one plate of lunch really cost?
steps.tip: This is the 'aha' from the lesson: one sandwich costs $2.50 on paper, but the store wants $15 for the packages.

levels.explore: Find the price of 3 packages on the Price Menu or a flyer, and add them on a calculator.
levels.develop: Price the whole list by package, then work out what one serving of one meal really costs.
levels.extend: Price one sandwich (2 bread, 2 turkey, 1 cheese) from the packages. Why isn't it $2.50 or $15?

steps.title: Shop it
steps.why: Their list, their basket, real prices on the shelf.
steps.kid: At the store, your kid shops from their own list and checks each shelf price against their plan. When there's a bigger size, they decide if it's really a deal: cheaper per serving only counts if you'll use it before it goes off. Before the till, they estimate the total, then compare it with the receipt.
steps.you: Push the cart and stay out of the choices. If something is missing or costs more, ask what they'd swap and let them decide.
ask: Is the big pack a deal if half of it gets thrown out?
How close was your estimate to the till?
steps.tip: Rounding each price to the nearest dollar as it goes in the basket makes the estimate quick, and usually close.

levels.explore: Find 3 things from the list in the store and put them in the basket yourself.
levels.develop: Shop the whole list, compare one bigger and smaller size, and estimate the total before the till.
levels.extend: For one bigger size, work out how much you'd have to use before it beats the small one, and decide if you will.

steps.title: Cook it and check the plan
steps.why: The meal is the test. The receipt and the leftovers are the results.
steps.kid: Your kid helps make the meals, from washing and stirring to setting the table. Afterward, they check the plan: were there enough plates of food, what's left over, and how does the receipt compare with the priced list? Then they work out what one meal cost per person.
steps.you: You handle the hot and sharp jobs. They do everything else they can, and they serve it. Ask about the leftovers before anything goes in the fridge.
ask: Did everyone get enough, or was there lots left?
What did one person's dinner cost?
steps.tip: Leftovers aren't waste if they have a plan. Ask where they'll go: tomorrow's lunch, a snack, the freezer.

levels.explore: Help make one meal, and count how many plates it filled.
levels.develop: Make the meals, compare the receipt with the plan and work out the cost per person for one meal.
levels.extend: Work out what the leftovers cost, and plan how they get eaten before they're wasted.

reference.title: Price Menu
reference.intro: Ballpark prices for when you can't check a flyer or website. Use package prices for the shopping list (Step 3) and per-serving prices to see what one plate costs. Real local prices are even better.

conclusion.headline: The plan survived the store.
conclusion.text: On the next grocery run, hand them one item, like yogurt, and ask which is cheaper per serving: single cups or the tub of 6. They'll divide before they answer. Expect them to check the fridge before anything goes in the cart.
conclusion.celebrate: Name the leftover they planned for: 'Tomorrow's toast comes out of today's loaf. Nothing wasted. Good catch.'
extensions: Plan the same meals on half the budget
Add a constraint: travel-friendly, no cooking or minimal waste
Plan a week of packed lunches using shared ingredients
Let them plan and shop one meal every week

signs: They ask how many servings are in a package
They check what's at home before writing a list
They notice when a bigger size is the better deal
makeItReal: Put one meal a week on the calendar as theirs to plan, shop and make. Keep the receipts in a folder, and compare the cost per person after a month.
levelsLine: Every step has three levels: Explore, Develop, Extend. Pick the one that fits your kid today, and change it anytime. Siblings can do the same step at different levels, side by side.

fromHome.text: My kids each plan one meal a week: they find a recipe, list the ingredients and make it. In the spring they hosted a board game afternoon for friends and planned the food themselves: mini pizzas and a veggie tray. They wrote the list, did the shopping with a basket, and made all of it.
